messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 44

# The Sound He Can't Unhear

Marco is a 35-year-old Colombian-born guitarist who has spent the better part of his adult life playing in restaurants, wedding halls, and small concert venues across the city. Music has always been the language he trusts most — more reliable, he says, than words. He met his wife, Daniela, at one of his shows eight years ago, and they married two years later. Until eighteen months ago, his life moved more or less the way he had always imagined it would.

The accident happened on a Tuesday evening in November. Marco was driving home after a late rehearsal, his guitar in the back seat, when a commercial truck ran a red light and struck the driver's side of his car at full speed. The car spun, rolled, and came to rest against a concrete barrier. Marco remembers the sound of the impact — a grinding, tearing roar — and then a strange, suspended silence before the pain arrived. He was conscious throughout. He lay pinned in the wreckage for nearly forty minutes, certain, in the way that feels absolute and animal, that he was going to die there. Rescue workers had to cut him out. He sustained a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and a severe laceration along his left forearm that required surgery. His left hand — his fretting hand — was spared, though it took weeks before he believed that fully.

Physically, Marco recovered. The bones healed. The scar on his forearm faded to a pale ridge. But something else did not heal on the same schedule, and this is what brings him in now.

He does not sleep well. Most nights he lies awake past two or three in the morning, his mind returning, unbidden, to the inside of that car — the smell of the airbag, the way the windshield looked after it shattered, the sound. It is always the sound that comes back hardest. He describes it as though it has been recorded somewhere inside his chest, playing on a loop he cannot switch off. When he does sleep, the dreams are vivid and violent, and he wakes with his heart slamming, reaching for Daniela, who has learned to simply put her hand on his back without asking questions.

Driving has become almost impossible. Marco sold his car four months after the accident and now takes the subway or asks Daniela to drive him. When he is in any vehicle, he sits rigid, watching every intersection, every merging lane, convinced that the next impact is already in motion. He has turned down gigs that require travel across town at night. He has turned down gigs for smaller reasons than that.

The music itself has changed. He still plays, because stopping entirely feels like a surrender he is not willing to make, but he notices that something has gone quiet in him when he picks up the guitar. He used to lose himself in it. Now he stays on the surface, technically competent but emotionally elsewhere. His bandmates have not said anything directly, but he has caught the looks they exchange. Daniela tells him his playing still sounds beautiful. He does not believe her, and the not-believing makes him feel guilty.

He finds himself irritable in ways that embarrass him — snapping at Daniela over small things, then feeling a wash of shame so intense it is almost physical. He has pulled back from his family, declining Sunday dinners at his in-laws' home, avoiding the noise and closeness that used to comfort him. He tells himself he is protecting them from a version of himself he does not fully recognize.

What Marco says, sitting in the chair across from his therapist, is that he feels like the accident broke something in him that the doctors could not see on any scan. He is not wrong that something broke. He is also not wrong, though he does not yet know it, that broken things can sometimes be repaired.
